title: Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays

concept.text: The innovation would be a comfortable, affordable display at the scale of ordinary glasses that places readable, stable digital information at useful depths within a person’s view of the real world. Achieving it requires combining convincing depth cues, adequate field of view, resolution and brightness, tolerance to eye movement, low power consumption and everyday wearability in one practical system. A laboratory improvement in one optical property is progress toward this capability, but does not establish the complete interface.

As a synthesis of the proposed capability, the environment could become a practical visual workspace: information could appear where it is useful, remain legible as the wearer looks around, and support tasks involving both nearby and distant content. Perceptual realism and practical usefulness are connected requirements. A convincing image that disappears with ordinary eye movement, or a readable overlay that cannot support comfortable extended use, would leave essential parts of the innovation unfinished.

significance.text: If the combined capability were achieved, its direct contribution would be an everyday display surface distributed through the wearer’s surroundings. Users could work with spatially placed information while retaining a view of the physical environment. The revolutionary prospect lies in making this arrangement broadly usable through comfort, accessibility and practical optical performance. The documented holographic work provides a technical basis for that prospect, but does not establish the proposed everyday capability or predict its adoption.

As a conditional impact assessment, richer applications could include remote presence, shared workspaces and location-aware assistance. These would also require capable capture, tracking, interaction and social design. A spatial display alone would not provide convincing remote participants, reliably understand a location or coordinate a group’s activity. Likewise, describing the environment as a workspace does not imply that every surface becomes equally usable, that virtual content becomes physically tangible, or that conventional displays cease to be useful.

The relevant scale of advance is the integrated experience. A larger region in which an image remains visible, a thinner optical stack or an improved depth demonstration can remove an important obstacle without resolving affordability, battery life, comfort or stable placement of content in the world. The 2025 prototype should therefore be interpreted as an enabling optical advance, with everyday impact conditional on further integration and evaluation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is simultaneous delivery of perceptually convincing spatial imagery and practical everyday wear. The supplied paper documents coupled requirements involving compactness, realistic depth, field of view, image quality and tolerance to pupil movement. Its discussion of brightness and low power describes promises of holographic technology rather than demonstrated performance of a complete all-day system. The available evidence identifies these engineering challenges without establishing that every relevant approach remained unsolved across the field in November 2026.

A central optical barrier is balancing field of view with the eyebox—the region in which the wearer’s pupil can receive the intended image. A useful display must accommodate different facial anatomies, ordinary eye movements and some movement of the glasses on the head. Enlarging this region while preserving image quality, depth presentation and a compact form factor is therefore part of accessibility and robustness, rather than merely a specification improvement.

As an integration assessment, the remaining work also includes delivering adequate brightness across indoor and outdoor conditions, sustaining computation and display operation within a wearable power budget, and maintaining comfort over full working days. Stable content placement adds tracking and system requirements beyond the optical display. These properties must work together on the same device: evidence collected from different apparatuses or operating conditions cannot by itself establish their simultaneous achievement.

current_state.text: Spatial displays and mixed-reality systems already exist, and holographic prototypes have made relevant progress. The supplied review verified the identity and retained full text of Suyeon Choi, Changwon Jang, Douglas Lanman and Gordon Wetzstein’s “Synthetic Aperture Waveguide Holography for Compact Mixed-Reality Displays with Large Étendue,” published in Nature Photonics on 28 July 2025, DOI: 10.1038/s41566-025-01718-w. It reports a compact prototype with a 9 × 8 mm eyebox and a 38° diagonal field of view. These are reported prototype specifications supported by the supplied textual review; they are not evidence of an independently replicated everyday product.

The reported approximately 3 mm thickness refers to the optical stack from the spatial light modulator to the eyepiece, rather than the thickness of an entire untethered device. The Methods distinguish a compact prototype used for Figures 1 and 2 from a benchtop apparatus used for Figures 3 and 4. Figure 4’s colour images are described in the text as pseudo-colour composites. Consequently, the measurements and demonstrations should not be combined into an inference that one thin, wearable device delivered every illustrated capability, including integrated full-colour operation.

The retained HTML and PDF allowed the supplied review to verify the 2025 paper’s textual claims, superseding the earlier research account that the article and PDF could not be opened. The review did not visually inspect the figures or inspect linked supplementary material. It also did not inspect a full-day user study. The reported optical results therefore do not establish affordable manufacture, full-day battery life, comfort in everyday use or stable world-anchored tracking. The paper’s path toward holographic mixed-reality glasses remains distinct from demonstration of the complete proposed interface.

The earlier research also identified a purported article titled “End-to-End Design for Full-Color and Large Field-of-View Computational Holographic Displays,” dated 24 September 2026 and associated with DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78029-3. The supplied artifact for its PubMed URL contains only a cookie interstitial, with no usable title, authors, publication date, DOI or abstract. Its identity, date and scientific results therefore remain unverified. The source-index title cannot substitute for article content, and the access obstruction neither disproves the purported result nor weakens the separately verified 2025 result.

Evidence limitation: the supplied freshness record is empty, so these materials do not support a comprehensive account of the field as of 1 November 2026. They establish a dated 2025 prototype advance and an unresolved later citation. They do not establish either that the full everyday capability has been achieved or that no other work has achieved it.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently evaluate complete, untethered glasses over full working days with a varied population, indoors and outdoors. Participants should reliably read and manipulate stable content across near and far depths, including during ordinary eye movement and modest device slippage. This proposal operationalizes the documented goals of all-day wear, realistic imagery and accessibility across users; it is not a published standard prescribed by the cited paper.
completion_criteria.label: Untethered glasses support reliable depth-spanning interaction throughout full working days

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation protocol: define task-success, readability, spatial-stability, comfort and affordability thresholds before testing. Compare visual comfort and usability with appropriate conventional displays on matched tasks. Report field of view, resolution, brightness, supported depths, eyebox and practical optical limitations alongside mass, battery life and realistic manufacturing cost. Measure the properties on the same integrated system, identifying any separate configurations or demonstrations that support only part of the claim.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated-system evaluation reports predefined thresholds, comparative usability and resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: make the device configuration, operating conditions, tasks, participant coverage and analysis sufficiently explicit for independent repetition. Report failures and restrictions, including conditions or users for whom content becomes unreadable, unstable or uncomfortable. Replicated success across the tested users and environments would establish demonstrated breadth of everyday usefulness; finite testing would not establish literal universality or remove the need to state practical boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Independent repetition is enabled and practical boundaries are reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” has the closest application overlap. HCI-07 could provide a visual medium for shared spatial content, while HCI-11 concerns whether collaborators receive useful social and spatial cues. Better display optics would not alone establish effective remote collaboration. HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” addresses a complementary sensory and interaction capability: visually convincing content does not supply convincing touch or force.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could inform the evaluation and design of spatial interfaces, whereas HCI-07 concerns achieving a particular display capability. HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality,” concerns access to software across modalities. A spatial display would be one possible presentation medium, but its optical accessibility across different users would not by itself make software operable through each user’s chosen modality.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” and HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” concern communication and control capabilities that could use spatial displays. Neither follows from a convincing visual display: reliable control after paralysis and conversational translation across languages require their own capabilities and evidence.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” could support user-created spatial tools, while HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” could govern work presented through such tools. HCI-07 supplies a possible visual workspace; understandable programming and meaningful control over delegated activity remain separate interface problems.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” could present contextual recollections through spatial displays, but requires memory and evidence-control capabilities beyond the display. HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” concerns how information use is understood and governed across services. Everyday spatial presentation may create settings in which those controls matter, without supplying them. These roster entries remain distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: The purported 2026 article’s identity, publication date, DOI association and results remain unverified because the supplied artifact contains only a cookie interstitial.
The supplied evidence does not resolve the broader state of the field as of 1 November 2026.
The reviewed 2025 material does not establish affordability, full-day battery life, everyday comfort or stable world-anchored tracking in a complete untethered device.
Figure imagery and linked supplementary material were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting assessment of details beyond the verified text.
A future evaluation must specify numerical task-success, stability, comfort and affordability thresholds, participant coverage and operating conditions; no established thresholds are supplied here.

brief.title: Everyday glasses that put digital information in view
possible: You could read and move digital information placed around your surroundings while still seeing the real world. Comfortable, affordable glasses would keep nearby and distant content readable and steady as you looked around, throughout a working day.
why: Your surroundings could become a practical workspace, with information appearing where you need it. People could work with digital content while keeping the physical task or place in view.

sources.who: Suyeon Choi, Changwon Jang, Douglas Lanman and Gordon Wetzstein
sources.showed: They built a compact display using holography, which shapes light to create images with depth. Their design expanded the region where the eye can see the image, and their light-modeling software improved image quality.
sources.quote: Our implicit model achieves superior quality compared with existing methods; it requires an order of magnitude less training data and time than existing CNN model architectures
sources.cited_for: This work supports a path toward thin displays that preserve depth cues as the eye moves.
sources.not_established: The prototypes do not establish comfortable, affordable glasses with all-day battery life and content that stays fixed in the surroundings.

sources.who: Yongdong Wang, Tong Yang, Dewen Cheng and Yongtian Wang
sources.showed: They built full-colour displays worn near the eyes, offering a wide view and depth. Designing the light patterns and lenses together corrected colour errors, optical blur and distortion.
sources.quote: Two prototypes, a full-color, large depth-of-field (DOF), large field-of-view (FOV) holographic near-eye display and a full-color, large FOV, multi-focus 3D holographic freeform augmented-reality (AR) near-eye display, validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework
sources.cited_for: This work supports designing the light patterns and physical lenses together to improve colour and depth.
sources.not_established: The prototypes do not establish a complete pair of everyday glasses that combines these optical results with practical wearability.

shown: Choi and colleagues built a compact prototype with an image-forming optical stack about 3 mm thick. That measurement describes the optics, rather than a complete pair of glasses. Some depth and image demonstrations used a separate laboratory setup.
Wang and colleagues demonstrated full-colour prototypes with a wide view and depth. These results extend the optical capabilities demonstrated, but do not establish the combined everyday experience.
missing: One complete device still needs to combine convincing depth, clear images, useful brightness and reliable viewing during eye movement or glasses slippage.
The same glasses need to sustain comfortable use, battery power and stable content placement throughout a working day at an affordable cost.
Independent testing needs to establish which users and environments the complete system serves reliably.

milestones.label: Untethered glasses support reliable interaction throughout working days
milestones.explanation: Independent full-day trials would have to show varied users reading and moving stable near and far content indoors and outdoors, despite eye movement and glasses slippage. This would establish practical everyday use.

milestones.label: One system meets predefined performance and usability thresholds
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to set success thresholds beforehand, compare matched tasks with conventional displays, and report optical performance, comfort, mass, battery life and cost on the same system. This would expose practical tradeoffs.

milestones.label: Independent teams repeat success and report practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat results using explicit device, task, participant and operating details, with failures reported. This would establish how broadly the glasses work and where their usefulness ends.

uncertain: The task success, readability, stability, comfort and affordability thresholds needed to count as success remain undefined.
How much variation across users and environments would demonstrate broad everyday usefulness remains an open judgment.

page.title: All-day optical see-through augmented reality glasses
page.definition: The wearer looks through transparent optics at the surroundings. The glasses add colour 3D images that stay aligned with physical locations as the head moves. A virtual object appears in focus at the same distance at which the two eyes turn toward it. One pair provides these functions indoors and outdoors throughout a waking day on one charge. For comparison, Snap rates its see-through SPECS glasses for up to four hours of mixed use per charge.

goal.need: Assemblers and fabricators held about 1.8 million US jobs in 2025. Reading a diagram on paper or a screen leaves the worker to work out where each part goes and which way it faces. Glasses can show the placement directly on the workpiece while keeping both hands free. In a 75-person trial with a 56-step block assembly, aligned instructions cut the error rate by 82%, chiefly by preventing one mistake from causing others. Completion times were comparable to those with screen-based computer guidance.

figures.caption: Reported specifications of Choi et al.'s compact prototype
figures.note: Eyebox means the region from which the entire image is visible. Optical-stack thickness excludes a complete glasses assembly.

statements.context: Meta describes the intended form of true augmented reality glasses.

statements.quote: users cannot discern virtual objects from real objects.
statements.context: The report states its expectation for truly immersive augmented reality, particularly mixed reality; it does not define a psychophysical acceptance protocol.

statements.quote: Building at scale to make them more affordable
statements.context: One of Meta's stated development priorities after presenting Orion.
Grant agreement 101135770, signed on 15 November 2023, includes prescription correction and comfort during daily activities.

completion.title: One cable-free pair meets the display and tracking targets indoors and outdoors for a waking day on one charge.
completion.criterion: One cable-free optical see-through glasses system simultaneously supplies matched accommodation and vergence cues, RGB imagery at ≥60 Hz and 1.5K × 1K pixels per eye across 30° × 20°, position error <1 cm, rotational accuracy 0.25°, and motion-to-photon latency <20 ms. It delivers 10,000–100,000 cd/m² virtual-image luminance outdoors with <1 W on-glasses power. These functions remain available during indoor and outdoor spatial tasks throughout an observed waking day without recharging.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional integration of selected 3GPP engineering targets and Meta's wearability objective.
completion.basis: 3GPP supplies the component targets. IEC specifies eyewear displays and methods for measuring image quality. The Atlas combines selected targets with an observed waking day on one charge. Snap's 20-hour mixed-use figure includes four case recharges. Yun and colleagues demonstrated outdoor imagery and describe their prototype as a mock-up in their published author response.

milestones.title: A see-through display supplies matching focus and binocular depth cues.
milestones.criterion: For virtual targets depicted at different distances, the optical focus distance follows the distance specified by the left-eye and right-eye views. A real target and a virtual target placed at the same depth require the same focus.

milestones.title: An AR display provides 1.5K × 1K pixels per eye over 30° × 20°.
milestones.criterion: Each eye receives an RGB image of at least 1.5K × 1K pixels across a 30° horizontal by 20° vertical field, with a display refresh rate of at least 60 Hz.
milestones.set_by: 3GPP, TR 26.998 V18.1.0, Table 4.5.2-1, Spatial Resolution per eye, Field of View, Colour and Display refresh rate.

milestones.title: AR tracking errors fall below 1 cm, with motion-to-photon latency below 20 ms.
milestones.criterion: Six-degree-of-freedom tracking attains the stated translation threshold and the desired rotational accuracy of 0.25°. Motion-to-photon latency measures the delay from movement to the corresponding displayed update.
milestones.set_by: 3GPP, TR 26.998 V18.1.0, Table 4.5.2-1. The combined tracking and latency targets are stated in the table.

milestones.title: One pair of AR glasses meets optical and tracking targets outdoors below 1 W.
milestones.criterion: In outdoor operation, one wearable prototype simultaneously supplies matched focus and binocular depth cues, RGB imagery at ≥60 Hz and ≥1.5K × 1K pixels per eye across 30° × 20°, six-degree-of-freedom tracking with translation error <1 cm and rotation error ≤0.25°, and motion-to-photon latency <20 ms. Virtual-image luminance is 10,000–100,000 cd/m² and power consumed on the glasses is <1 W.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. No external body identified sets this combined prototype test. Its component targets come from 3GPP TR 26.998 V18.1.0, Table 4.5.2-1.

milestones.title: A see-through display keeps a virtual object aligned with a physical location as the wearer moves.
milestones.criterion: Through the display, the wearer sees a physical reference and a virtual object at the same location. As the wearer changes viewpoint, the display updates the perspective in real time so the virtual object stays aligned with the reference in three dimensions.
milestones.set_by: The field's convention for real-time 3D registration, stated by Ronald T. Azuma in A Survey of Augmented Reality.
milestones.threshold_quote:
1) Combines real and virtual
2) Interactive in real time
3) Registered in 3-D

milestones.title: Head tracking achieves sub-centimetre position accuracy and quarter-degree rotation accuracy.
milestones.criterion: Track head position and orientation in six degrees of freedom. Relative to a reference pose, translational error is below 1 cm and rotational error is at most 0.25°.
milestones.set_by: 3GPP, TR 26.998 V18.1.0, Table 4.5.2-1, Tracking. The report describes quarter-degree rotation accuracy as desired.

milestones.title: The see-through display updates in less than 20 ms after head motion.
milestones.criterion: Measure the elapsed time from physical head motion to the corresponding change in light emitted by the display. This end-to-end motion-to-photon latency is below 20 ms.

not_found: No published numerical acceptance thresholds for day-long wear, comfort or affordability were found.
The full IEC 63145-10:2023 and IEC 63145-22-20:2024 texts were not accessible from their public catalogue pages.
No published waking-day trial was found that measured the combined optical, tracking and on-glasses power targets on one charge.
No standards-body or professional-society statement was found that judges all-day optical see-through AR glasses infeasible or unworthy of pursuit.

results.quote: Verified by advanced robotic measurement systems, SPECS deliver 7-millisecond motion-to-photon latency, helping digital content feel anchored in the real world.

results.finding: Among five commercial XR devices tested across 16 scenarios, Apple Vision Pro had the lowest mean translational relative pose error at 0.52 cm.
results.detail: Relative pose error was measured over 10 cm segments, with each segment realigned to Vicon at its start. Absolute pose error used one alignment for the entire trajectory.
results.quote: across all experiments, the AVP consistently outperformed its peers, achieving an average RPE of 0.52 cm and APE of 3.62 cm.

results.finding: Across 3 motion datasets, inertial prediction in the optical see-through HMD was 5–10 times more accurate on average than no prediction.
results.detail: The prototype used one eye and one calibrated wooden frame. The motion datasets covered walking, head rotation, and fast combined motion. Dynamic errors were quantified from recorded tracker data and a modeled screen projection.
results.quote:
On average, our inertial-based
predictor is 5-10 times more accurate than doing no prediction and
2-3 times more accurate than prediction without inertial sensors.

results.finding: HoloLens 2 translation, one bench trial per condition across three marker types, yielded mean horizontal trajectory RMSE up to 0.56 mm.
results.detail: Dynamic time warping compares relative horizontal trajectories and can accommodate timing differences. The setup used a fixed nominal target distance and a camera at the right-eye position.

results.finding: The IG-1005 see-through headset matched optical focus to binocular depth at 3 distances in a study of 40 participants.
results.detail: The match was demonstrated at discrete focal planes. The study assessed optical stimulus demands and perceptual distance judgments. Participants’ accommodation and vergence responses were unmeasured.
results.quote: In the consistent-cues condition, the images were displayed at the focal distances of planes that coincided with the rendered image distances.

results.finding: The ZD-72/S headset (one model, test sample size unspecified) is rated at 2048 × 2048 full-color pixels per eye.
results.detail: The figures are manufacturer specifications. The source gives no independent measurements or details of the display’s color architecture.

title = "All-day optical see-through augmented reality glasses". Reason: The current title also describes glasses already available, while the entry sets all-day operation as its goal.

definition = "The wearer looks through transparent optics at the surroundings. The glasses add colour 3D images that stay aligned with physical locations as the head moves. A virtual object appears in focus at the same distance at which the two eyes turn toward it. One pair provides these functions indoors and outdoors throughout a waking day on one charge. For comparison, Snap rates its see-through SPECS glasses for up to four hours of mixed use per charge.". Reason: The definition can explain what matching depth cues mean to the wearer and give a concrete comparison for all-day operation.

goal.need = "Assemblers and fabricators held about 1.8 million US jobs in 2025. Reading a diagram on paper or a screen leaves the worker to work out where each part goes and which way it faces. Glasses can show the placement directly on the workpiece while keeping both hands free. In a 75-person trial with a 56-step block assembly, aligned instructions cut the error rate by 82%, chiefly by preventing one mistake from causing others. Completion times were comparable to those with screen-based computer guidance.". Reason: The current rationale gives an optical resolution measurement without explaining who benefits or what they could do better.
add statement by Horizon Europe, POPULAR project, 2023: "suitable for all-day use". Reason: The POPULAR grant supplies a public research programme's explicit all-day eyewear objective.

edit completion: title = "One cable-free pair meets the display and tracking targets indoors and outdoors for a waking day on one charge."; basis = "3GPP supplies the component targets. IEC specifies eyewear displays and methods for measuring image quality. The Atlas combines selected targets with an observed waking day on one charge. Snap's 20-hour mixed-use figure includes four case recharges. Yun and colleagues demonstrated outdoor imagery and describe their prototype as a mock-up in their published author response."; refs = [2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 13, 19]. Reason: The title uses “untethered” where the criterion specifies cable-free operation, and the published near misses clarify what the duration requirement tests.
